time.desc: The short video platform and its parent company filed a lawsuit in federal court, legally challenging the federal law of "forced stripping or banning" and claiming that it violated the right to free speech.
A group of content creators is suing the government in an attempt to block a federal "stripping or banning" law from taking effect, citing harm to free speech.
Federal appeals court issues and adopts expedited timetable to move forward with litigation over "strike or ban" law

The platform announced restrictions on the recommendation and placement of content from media accounts with certain national backgrounds overseas in response to disputes over the influence of information during the election period.

The federal government filed documents with the Court of Appeal outlining the national security threats posed by the platform and disclosing intelligence allegations that it cooperated with foreign censorship and data access.
The federal government and regulators filed a civil lawsuit against the platform, accusing it of a long history of violating children's privacy laws and collecting data from minors.
The federal appeals court held its first oral argument on the "strike or ban" law, and the two sides launched a court battle over free speech and national security.

Multiple state attorneys general jointly sued the platform, accusing it of harming the physical and mental health of minors through the design of addictive products and misleading the public about safety measures.

The government of an allied country ordered the closure of the platform's corporate operations in the country based on the conclusion of the national security review. The platform stated that it would initiate a legal challenge
The federal appeals court ruled to uphold the "strike or ban" law and gave a compliance cutoff. The platform announced that it would continue to appeal to the Supreme Court to seek overturn.
The platform submitted an emergency injunction application to the court, requesting to suspend the implementation of the ban measures that will take effect pending the hearing of the Supreme Court.

A former platform marketing executive files an amended lawsuit alleging that the parent company has far more control over the platform than publicly acknowledged and that the CEO is merely a sounding board.
Digital rights and civil liberties groups file an amicus brief with the court arguing that a state’s ban on the platform violates free speech
Major rival companies hit record highs in lobbying spending in a single quarter and are accused of secretly pushing for legislation against the platform
A real estate tycoon teamed up with an investment bank to form a consortium to bid for the platform business and proposed a data open source reconstruction plan
The platform and the regulatory agency jointly applied to the court to speed up the trial of the litigation case and proposed key time points.
The platform began to develop its own independent version of the core algorithm to isolate domestic user data and alleviate data security concerns.
A presidential candidate officially joined the short video platform and posted his first video. The number of followers on his account exceeded millions within two days.

A super political action committee (super PAC) supporting Leader A officially settled in Platform X and opened an official account, announcing that it would spread the candidate's campaign agenda of "supporting freedom and supporting Country A" on a daily basis.

Platform X confirmed that its security team discovered a zero-day vulnerability attack targeting brand and celebrity accounts. The malicious code was spread through the platform's private message function, and users were infected when they opened the message without any action. Official accounts such as Media I, Eighteen and Company L were compromised. The platform said that the number of affected accounts was "very small" and it was assisting in restoring access.

Institution B filed legal documents with a federal appeals court, and for the first time, national intelligence officials publicly alleged that Platform X and Parent Company Y had censored foreign content at the request of Institution G, and accused its employees of sharing sensitive data of Country A users on internal communication tool A, making the data stored on Country B servers and accessible to domestic employees; Platform X denied the accusation and said the government never provided evidence.

Institution M Chief Administrative Officer Twenty has issued an internal notice, announcing that it will ban and remove all Company Y applications on Institution M management devices within a time limit. Newly banned editing application A, photo retouching application A, internal communication tool A and Photo App A will be removed. The mobile version will be removed first. This move extends the previously implemented Platform X ban.
